source.title: Language in the Flow of Time: Time-Series-Paired Texts Weaved into a Unified Temporal Narrative
source.authors: Zihao Li; Xiao Lin; Zhi-Ning Liu; Jiaru Zou; Zi-Wei Wu; Lecheng Zheng; Dong-Qi Fu; Ya-Da Zhu; Hendrik Hamann; Hanghang Tong; Jing-Rui He

record.file_problem: None noted; the supplied text includes the paper and appendices through the final page.
record.tranche_reason: Measures cross-modal alignment and its dependence on data pairing and metric settings using spectral periodicity and TT-Wasserstein, rather than testing the claim's model-scaling or representation-distance method.
record.gate_note: The study measures periodicity alignment between timestamp-paired text and time series, including original and shuffled data and TT-Wasserstein configuration sensitivity. Forecasting and imputation scores are not rows because they measure predictive performance, not representation convergence.
record.test_reason: The study invokes the Platonic Representation Hypothesis only as motivation. Its alignment measure, TT-Wasserstein, compares the Fourier spectrum of a raw numerical time series with the lag-similarity spectrum of one text encoder's embeddings (GPT-2). That is temporal-periodicity agreement between a data signal and one model's embeddings. It is not similarity between two models' representations of paired inputs. No model pair, scale series, seed comparison, mapping, shared-feature analysis or alternative representation-similarity metric is reported. The bulk of the results is the TaTS method's forecasting and imputation performance. The CTR measurements are a related but different construct, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. The reader's V6 links and labels do not hold.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors, motivated by the PRH, report that time-series-paired texts can show periodic patterns matching the series (CTR), measurable with TT-Wasserstein. Lower TT-Wasserstein ratios tend to accompany larger TaTS gains within a sampling frequency, with Climate an exception. Their main conclusion is that TaTS, which treats projected text embeddings as auxiliary variables, improves forecasting and imputation across nine backbones and 18 datasets. They attribute CTR to shared external drivers, texts responding to the series, and related variables mentioned in the texts.
record.recipe_differences: Measures spectral periodicity alignment between paired time series and text embeddings, rather than model-to-model distances or representation convergence across scale.
record.method_sensitivity: TT-Wasserstein values are generally stable across tested windowing, normalization, and frequency-resolution configurations; original versus timestamp-shuffled inputs yield larger distances.

fits_no_version.finding: Time-series-paired text embeddings (GPT-2, mean-pooled) show lag-similarity periodicities that match the dominant frequencies of the paired numerical series, e.g. period 12 in monthly data (Fig. 2). The spectral Wasserstein distance is lower for original than for timestamp-shuffled pairings in most Time-MMD datasets: e.g. Economy 0.022 vs 0.098/0.099, Traffic 0.035 vs 0.102/0.104. It is nearly unchanged for Security, Energy and Health, where differences fall within the bootstrap SDs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embeddings of timestamp-aligned text inherit the periodic structure of the paired numerical time series (Chronological Textual Resonance). The degree of this spectral agreement depends on dataset and text relevance.

record.problems: The evidence concerns periodic spectra of paired text and time series, not similarity between independently trained model representations. The authors state that they do not investigate data-construction factors that may induce the alignment, and that generalization to other modalities such as paired images or audio is untested. The metric sensitivity analysis reports block-bootstrap standard deviations, but Table 11 gives them without additional methodological detail in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Forecasting and imputation results, encoder comparisons, and other TaTS performance ablations were not included because they measure predictive performance rather than representation convergence. Table 10's individual per-dataset configuration values are represented by the authors' aggregate stability statement in R28.

untested.parts: All: no comparison of independently trained models, and no scale or capability axis for alignment.
All: no vision-language models and no image-caption pairs. Alignment is not tracked against model quality; the encoder swaps (BERT, GPT-2, LLaMA2) report forecasting MSE only.
All: no cross-model mapping or stitching. The TaTS MLP projects text embeddings for forecasting and is not evaluated as a representation map.
All: no feature or circuit analysis.
All as worded: no representation-similarity measure across models is varied, and no out-of-distribution test of model convergence is run.
All: no measure of model-model alignment, so no test of completeness, plateau or causes.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed. V6 concerns how measured convergence between model representations depends on the metric and inputs. Here the shuffles are a validity check for a data-vs-embedding periodicity score, and only one text encoder is used for CTR. Even on its own terms, the shuffle effect is weak or absent for Security, Energy and Health, with differences smaller than the Table 11 bootstrap SDs. Table 10 shows sizeable configuration swings despite the authors' stability claim. No result here should be read as evidence for or against the PRH.

versions.untested_parts: Model scale, capability, and convergence across independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
Vision-language models on paired images and captions, and alignment rising with model quality.
Convergence across random seeds, shared features, and subspaces.
Mapping or stitching representations across models, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.

The study tests input shuffling and TT-Wasserstein configuration choices, but not alternative representation-similarity measures, out-of-distribution inputs, or convergence between model representations.
Whether shared training data or objectives explain model-representation alignment, or whether it plateaus or remains incomplete.

rows.subject: Time-MMD datasets (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied spectral windowing, normalization, and frequency resolution for TT-Wasserstein.

conditions.value: Windowing schemes, normalization strategies, and frequency resolutions varied one at a time

rows.baseline: Default: rectangular window, ℓ1-normalization, native FFT resolution
rows.value: Authors report the metric is generally stable across configuration choices.
rows.note: Aggregate textual conclusion; the table gives per-dataset values for each configuration.
rows.check: This is sensitivity of the study's own periodicity metric, not of a representation-convergence measure. The authors' 'generally stable' wording is also generous. Table 10 shows Agriculture moving from 0.026 to between 0.011 and 0.061, and Health from 0.233 to 0.170.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: TT-Wasserstein is higher after either shuffle than on the original data across the nine listed datasets, indicating that the measured alignment responds to input pairing (R02–R03, R05–R06, R08–R09, R11–R12, R14–R15, R17–R18, R20–R21, R23–R24, R26–R27).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tested TT-Wasserstein windowing, normalization, and frequency-resolution choices
reader_labels.reason: The authors describe the metric as generally stable across the tested configurations, qualifying any claim that alignment necessarily weakens substantially under reasonable settings (R28).
